ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Raw audio and narratives cannot be shared publicly because these data contain potentially identifying information; ethical approval for this study permits these data to only be made available to other researchers upon reasonable request and with other measures enacted to protect participant confidentiality.
Ethics: This research was approved by the Baycrest Research Ethics Board (#19-07).
We recruited 53 young adults through the Rotman Research Institute Participant pool and community advertising.
Data from three participants were excluded due to distortions in audio recordings (n = 1) or task non-compliance (n = 2).
All participants gave written informed consent prior to testing and, upon completion, received $30 CAD.
During each trial, participants were presented with a detail set and the position of the location word (i.e., top, middle, bottom) was randomized across trials.
Before starting the task, participants completed one congruent and one incongruent practice trial and explained their rating choices to confirm their comprehension of the rating scales.
Participants completed all scales, but only the Analogy subscale was used for the current analyses.

For both fluency tasks, the relevant stimulus was shown onscreen and participants had one minute to list words beginning with a given letter (F, A, S) or belonging to a given category (animals, supermarket items).
To this end, we first collected descriptions of the 12 location schemas from a separate sample of participants (N = 20, aged 18-35 years, M = 27.85, SD = 4.15) recruited from Prolific.

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power software (Faul et al., 2009). The analysis used a published effect size for the correlation between episodic detail and the flexibility score of the AUT (Addis, Pan, et al., 2016), and determined that a minimum of 39 participants was required to achieve a power of at least .80, with an alpha level of .05. This result of this power analysis was reported in the pre-registration but due to a miscommunication, it misstated that the sample size would be 70. We had aimed for a larger sample size than N = 39 given the novelty of the text analyses, but the target was N=50.

prereg_check.title: Preregistration Check

table.title: Cognitive Processes Underlying Novel Future Thinking
table.research_questions:
We hypothesize that:

(1) (a) Schematicity and simulation success will be higher for congruent vs incongruent trials, and (b) schematicity will predict simulation success.

(2) higher executive functioning will predict (a) more successful simulation and (b) higher schematicity, (c) schematicity will mediate the effect of executive functioning on simulation success, and (d) the effects related to executive functions will be higher in the incongruent condition where demands on executive functioning are higher, whereas (e) the effect of schematicity on simulation success will be higher for congruent trials (i.e., moderation effects).
table.study_type: Experiment - A researcher randomly assigns treatments to study subjects, this includes field or lab experiments. This is also known as an intervention experiment and includes randomized controlled trials.
table.blinding: Personnel who analyze the data collected from the study are not aware of the treatment applied to any given group.
table.q5: With respect to the blinding of personnel during analysis selected above, this refers to raters who are undertaking Autobiographical Interview scoring of transcripts; they will be blind to condition, as well as participant such that each transcript from a participant will be assigned a separate blind code and scored in a random order.
table.study_design_overview: Within subjects design with 2 factors (trial type: congruent, incongruent). For analyses of Autobiographical Interview detail scores, detail type (internal vs. external/semantic) will be included as another within-subject factor.
table.existing_data: Registration prior to creation of data
table.data_collection_procedures:
Participants: Participants must be aged 18-35 years, fluent in English and have no history of psychiatric/neurological conditions. Participants will provide informed consent and will be paid $15/hr for their time.  

Future simulation paradigm: During each trial, participants will be presented with a detail-set (location and two objects) as cues to elicit imagined future events. Details will either be congruent or incongruent; presentation trials in these conditions will be randomized. Participants will be instructed to describe a future event integrating themselves and all three details together. They will describe each event aloud, which will be audio-recorded (and later transcribed for scoring). Following each imagination trials, participants will estimate the temporal distance of the event from the present, and provide ratings (on a 5-point scale) of: amount of detail and plausibility of the imagined event; similarity to previous experiences; and task difficulty. Following completion of the task, participants rate their familiarity with each location and object. 

Tasks measuring individual differences of executive functions: 
-	Test of Relational Reasoning (TORR; Alexander et al., 2016)
-	Alternate Uses Task (AUT; Guliford, 1967) 
-	Verbal fluency task (Troyer, 2000). 

Procedure: All tasks will be completed in one session (approximately 2 hours long). The order of the (1) simulation task and (2) individual differences tasks will be counterbalanced across participants.
table.sample_size: 90 younger adults (aged 18-35 years) will be recruited to obtain at least 70 useable datasets.
table.sample_size_rationale: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power software (Faul et al., 2007), based on a published effect size for the correlation between episodic detail and the Categories score of the AUT (Madore et al., 2015). This analysis determined we will need a minimum of 39 participants to achieve a power of at least .80, assuming an alpha error probability of .05.
table.manipulated_variables: Simulation Condition: We will manipulate the congruence of the location and object details used as cues, modulating the usefulness of location frameworks for scaffolding the integration of details into coherent events. To validate this manipulation, we had a previous online sample of participants (N = 25) rate how easy it was to create an event that integrated the objects and location and confirmed that ease of integration was higher for congruent versus incongruent trials. Importantly, semantic similarity of the words comprising the congruent vs. congruent stimuli did not differ to avoid differences in semantic similarity driving the ease of integration.
table.measured_variables:
Simulation success measures: 
(a)	Participants’ event narratives will be scored using the adapted Autobiographical Interview (AI) scoring protocol (Addis, Wong, & Schacter, 2008; Levine et al., 2002) to derive the number of internal, external and semantic details in each event narrative. While internal and external detail scores are our primary measures, we will also re-run analyses using semantic scores (cf. Devitt et al., 2017).
(b)	Participants’ subjective ratings of event detail and plausibility
Other measures:
(c)	Participants’ ratings of event novelty and simulation task difficulty will be used as manipulation checks. 
(d)	Participants estimated temporal distance of the simulated events, and word counts of event narratives will be used to rule out possible confounds.

Measure of schematicity: 
Using the Universal Sentence Encoder (USE; Cer et al., 2019), event narratives from the simulation task will be turned into a 512-dimension vectors. The vectors for participants’ event narratives will then be compared to vectors of schema templates (derived from descriptions of the location stimuli generated by an independent sample) using correlation measures (e.g. cosine similarity). Thus, the measure of schematicity for each trial is the correlation coefficient between event narrative vector and schema template vector.

Individual difference measures of executive function: 
-   The TORR has 4 subtests resulting in 4 subscores (analogical, anomalous, antinomous and antithetical reasoning) and a total score. Although our primary analyses will focus on the analogy subscore (see Indices), if there is insufficient variance in this subtest, we will use the TORR total score. 
-    Responses on the AUT will be scored using a standard scoring protocol (Madore et al., 2015), resulting in 5 scores (total uses, total appropriate uses, categories, categories of appropriate uses, elaboration and creativity). Although our primary analyses will focus on categories as a measure of flexibility (see Indices), if there is insufficient variance, we will use the total uses score.
-    Verbal fluency has 2 subtests: phonemic and semantic clustering, which will be scored using the scoring rules to derive mean cluster size for each (Troyer et al., 2000). Other scores from this measure are: raw number of switches, total number of correct words for semantic and phonemic verbal fluency (Troyer et al., 1997); we will also measure the total number of clusters for semantic and phonemic fluency. Although our primary analyses will focus on mean cluster size, our exploratory analyses will include raw number of switches, total correct words and total number of clusters (see Exploratory Analysis).
table.indices:
Analogical Reasoning Index:
We predict a high correlation between the TORR analogy score and AUT categories score. If so, we will collapse them together to create an “analogical reasoning index” to be used in the analyses below. To do this, we will z-transform these scores before averaging them. In the event that these two scores are not correlated, we will use them separately in the analyses.
table.statistical_tests:
Rule out confounds
-	Two-tailed paired t-test, IV: Condition, DV: Temporal Distance Rating
-	Two-tailed paired t-test, IV: Condition, DV:  Word count of event narratives

Manipulation checks 
-	One-tailed paired t-test, IV: Condition, DV: Difficulty Rating
-	One-tailed paired samples t-test, IV: Condition, DV: Novelty Rating

Hypothesis 1(a) Simulation success by condition
-	One-tailed paired samples t-test, IV: Condition, DV: Detail rating
-	One-tailed paired samples t-test, IV: Condition, DV: Plausibility rating
-	2 (Condition: Incongruent, Congruent) x 2 (AI Detail type: Internal, External) Repeated Measures ANOVA, DV: Number of details

Hypothesis 1(b) Schematicity by condition 
-	One-tailed paired samples t-test, IV: Condition, DV: Avg similarity

Hypothesis 2: 
-	Mediation Analysis:  executive functioning (X), simulation success (Y), schematicity (M), Condition (C)

table.transformations:
Prior to statistical analyses, we will conduct Shapiro-Wilk tests to ensure normal distribution within subjective ratings. In the event of a significant deviation, we will run a logarithmic or exponential transformation until normal.

We predict a high correlation between the TORR analogy score and AUT flexibility score. Consequently, we will collapse them together to create an “analogical reasoning metric” to be used in the analyses above. To do this, we will z-transform participant scores on these two measures. Equally weighted, the z-scores will be averaged to create an analogical reasoning metric.
table.inference_criteria: We will use the standard p < .05 threshold for determining rejection of the null hypothesis. We will adjust p-values for multiple comparisons using a Bonferroni correction as appropriate.
table.data_exclusion_criteria: Outliers will be excluded on a trial basis, if the event description is non-compliant to task instructions (i.e., a meaningless response is provided); if a future event is estimated as being more than 5 years into the future; and if the imagined event is as identical to a past experience (“5” on the similarity rating scale).
table.missing_data_handling: For simulation data, available trials will be used for analysis. If an individual difference measure is missing, the participant will excluded from all analyses, and (where possible) a replacement participant will be tested.
table.exploratory_analyses: As noted above, we may re-run analyses using the Semantic detail score from the Autobiographical Interview in place of the External detail score. We may also include the raw switching score, total number of clusters and total number of correct words from semantic and verbal fluency (or a composite score) as additional dependent variables in our mediation analysis. We will likely also examine whether schematicity is higher earlier in the simulation trials.

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .01", Text = "2 Congruent > Incongruent, p < .01."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Finally, an LMM predicting internal detail with a fixed effect of condition and a random intercept per participant showed that congruent future events had significantly more internal words (M = 394.00) compared to incongruent events (M = 371.00), (b = -22.26, t = -4.09, p < .001, β = -.10, 95% CI [-.15, -.05]; see Figure 1C).

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 127 columns across 8 data files.
#### Issues Identified

16 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 8 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: We recruited 53 young adults through the Rotman Research Institute Participant pool and community advertising.
Data from three participants were excluded due to distortions in audio recordings (n = 1) or task non-compliance (n = 2).
All participants gave written informed consent prior to testing and, upon completion, received $30 CAD.
During each trial, participants were presented with a detail set and the position of the location word (i.e., top, middle, bottom) was randomized across trials.
Before starting the task, participants completed one congruent and one incongruent practice trial and explained their rating choices to confirm their comprehension of the rating scales.
Participants completed all scales, but only the Analogy subscale was used for the current analyses.

For both fluency tasks, the relevant stimulus was shown onscreen and participants had one minute to list words beginning with a given letter (F, A, S) or belonging to a given category (animals, supermarket items).
To this end, we first collected descriptions of the 12 location schemas from a separate sample of participants (N = 20, aged 18-35 years, M = 27.85, SD = 4.15) recruited from Prolific.
To ensure they were members of the same collective group as the participants in the main sample, the Prolific sample only included individuals who were residents of Canada.
As in the main sample, these participants provided spoken narrative responses, albeit during a Zoom call rather than in-person.

To elicit schema descriptions, each location was presented on a PowerPoint slideshow and participants were instructed to describe each location as if they were preparing someone who had never been there: "What does it look like?
Where appropriate, mixed models with a random intercept per participant were used that account for the nested structure of the data.

As expected, participants gave higher difficulty ratings on incongruent trails compared to congruent trials (b = 0.47, z = 3.08, p = .002, OR = 1.61, 95% CI [1.18, 2.17]; see Supplemental Materials, Figure S1A).

Bonferroni-corrected pairwise contrasts revealed that, overall, participants had significantly higher perceptual (M = 0.16) compared to preparation schema use (M = 0.11; b = 0.05, t =12.91, p < .001), and significantly higher action (M = 0.15) compared to preparation schema use (b = 0.04, t = 10.79, p < .001).

Given that participants were instructed to narrate their reasoning process as well as the imagined event itself, detail ratings in this study may not have been not an ideal measure of simulation success.
In that validation study, 159 healthy adult participants (Mage = 29.83 years, SDage = 9.55, range: 18-67; 69 female) were recruited from Prolific.
All participants were fluent in English and reported a mean of 14.64 years of education (SD = 3.29).
Two participants were excluded due to task non-compliance (i.e., low effort as indicated by completing the study in < 10 mins or > 15 missing responses).
This task was a part of a one-hour online session that included other tasks, for which participants were compensated, on average, £5.24.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 1 R code file.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1L, File = "main-analyses.Rmd", "Runs after" = "—", 
    Basis = "none"), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**1 data path in the code does not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed it to where the file is, so the code could run: `sliding-window_schema_correlations-60.csv` to `data/sliding-window_schema_correlations-60.csv` (in main-analyses.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find the file. **2 data paths were built at runtime** with `sprintf()`/`paste()`/`file.path()` instead of written as a literal path — this is fragile authoring practice (it silently breaks if the code is run from a different working directory than the author's own). We resolved all of these on a best-effort basis.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 1 script: 0 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "main-analyses.Rmd", Outcome = "errored", 
    Detail = "undefined_variable", "Time (s)" = 41.2), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "main-analyses.Rmd", "Missing variable" = "condition_labels", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
**Calls that install packages in the code**

1 call to `install.packages()`, `groundhog`, `checkpoint`, `renv`, `pacman` and the like was replaced, since they install packages themselves: `groundhog.library()` and `p_load()` by `library()`, the others by a statement that does nothing. info.title: Building the future: Schemas contribute to episodic simulation
keywords: SLV: Conceptualization, Data curation, Formal Analysis, Investigation, Methodology, Validation, Visualization, Writing -Original Draft, Writing -Review & Editing

text.text: Future imagination is argued to rely on schematic knowledge and executive functions, yet direct evidence is lacking.
Participants (N=50) completed executive measures and imagined future events involving schema-congruent or -incongruent objects and locations.
Events were rated for detail and plausibility and scored for episodic content.

We also collected descriptions of the locations in a separate sample (N=20) that served as proxies for culturally-shared schemas in a narrative representational similarity analysis (RSA): schema and event texts were converted into highdimensional vectors using document embeddings, and cosine similarity was computed between vectors.
RSA showed evidence of schema use: event narratives were most similar in meaning to schema descriptions of the same locations, particularly at the start of trials.
Executive capacities were unrelated to schema use, although relational reasoning ability was associated with higher subjective detail on congruent trials.
This study provides initial direct evidence of schema use in service of future imagining.
Mentally simulating the future enables us to plan, make decisions, and solve problems (Schacter, 2012).
text.formatted: Mentally simulating the future enables us to plan, make decisions, and solve problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Schacter, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The constructive episodic simulation hypothesis posits that future simulation and episodic memory both rely on a core "simulation system" (Schacter & Addis, 2007), and indeed the two have similar phenomenology (D'Argembeau & Van Der Linden, 2004), developmental trajectories (Atance, 2008) and neural correlates (Benoit & Schacter, 2015).
text.formatted: The constructive episodic simulation hypothesis posits that future simulation and episodic memory both rely on a core "simulation system" <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">(Schacter & Addis, 2007)</ref>, and indeed the two have similar phenomenology <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(D'Argembeau & Van Der Linden, 2004)</ref>, developmental trajectories <ref type="bibr">(Atance, 2008)</ref> and neural correlates <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Benoit & Schacter, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Recently it has been suggested that future simulation also draws on schemas and, when an appropriate schema is unavailable, on executive functions such as relational reasoning (Addis, 2020a).
text.formatted: Recently it has been suggested that future simulation also draws on schemas and, when an appropriate schema is unavailable, on executive functions such as relational reasoning <ref type="bibr">(Addis, 2020a)</ref>.

text.text: The current study tested these hypotheses by manipulating the availability of relevant schemas and using a narrative form of representational similarity analysis (RSA) that leverages natural language processing to quantify schema use.
Schemas are cognitive structures that generalize across similar experiences, enabling both perception and prediction (Bartlett, 1932; Neisser, 1978).
text.formatted: Schemas are cognitive structures that generalize across similar experiences, enabling both perception and prediction <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bartlett, 1932;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Neisser, 1978)</ref>.

text.text: They do so in part by providing "scripts" for common situations (Schank & Abelson, 1977).
text.formatted: They do so in part by providing "scripts" for common situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Schank & Abelson, 1977)</ref>.

text.text: In episodic memory, schemas organize incoming information at encoding (Van Kesteren et al., 2012) and "fill in" details at retrieval (Gilboa & Marlatte, 2017; Gronau et al., 2008).
text.formatted: In episodic memory, schemas organize incoming information at encoding <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Van Kesteren et al., 2012)</ref> and "fill in" details at retrieval <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Gilboa & Marlatte, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Gronau et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, schemas may provide a predictive, flexible scaffold for constructing plausible future events (Addis, 2018 (Addis, , 2020a;; D'Argembeau & Demblon, 2012).
text.formatted: Similarly, schemas may provide a predictive, flexible scaffold for constructing plausible future events <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Addis, 2018</ref> <ref type="bibr">(Addis, , 2020a;;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">D'Argembeau & Demblon, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Empirically, individuals have well-developed schemas for familiar information (Van Kesteren et al., 2012) and familiarity with event cues is associated with both greater detail (Morales Valiente et al., 2025) and more script-like narration of future events (Cordonnier et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Empirically, individuals have well-developed schemas for familiar information <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">(Van Kesteren et al., 2012)</ref> and familiarity with event cues is associated with both greater detail <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Morales Valiente et al., 2025)</ref> and more script-like narration of future events <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Cordonnier et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Future simulation also recruits brain regions that mediate schemas, including the anterior hippocampus and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC: Benoit et al., 2014; Benoit & Schacter, 2015; D'Argembeau, 2013; Sheldon & Levine, 2016), and patients with vmPFC damage exhibit deficits in future simulation (e.g., Ciaramelli et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Future simulation also recruits brain regions that mediate schemas, including the anterior hippocampus and ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC: <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Benoit et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Benoit & Schacter, 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">D'Argembeau, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Sheldon & Levine, 2016)</ref>, and patients with vmPFC damage exhibit deficits in future simulation (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Ciaramelli et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Spatial schemas may be particularly important, defining the actions, actors and objects expected in a location (Gronau et al., 2008; B. Tversky & Hemenway, 1983).
text.formatted: Spatial schemas may be particularly important, defining the actions, actors and objects expected in a location <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Gronau et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">B. Tversky & Hemenway, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, events imagined in familiar spatial contexts are more detailed (Robin, 2018) and vivid (D'Argembeau & Van Der Linden, 2012).
text.formatted: Indeed, events imagined in familiar spatial contexts are more detailed <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">(Robin, 2018)</ref> and vivid <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(D'Argembeau & Van Der Linden, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: When imagining novel situations, however, a relevant schema may not be available.

Thus, executive processes may be required to expand upon existing knowledge to create new schemas and to search for relevant episodic details (Addis, 2020a; Addis et al., 2025; Sheldon & Levine, 2016).
text.formatted: Thus, executive processes may be required to expand upon existing knowledge to create new schemas and to search for relevant episodic details <ref type="bibr">(Addis, 2020a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Addis et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">Sheldon & Levine, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Strategic search abilities, such as the clustered generation of outputs on fluency or retrieval tasks, has been related to the ability to imagine specific and detailed future events (Addis, Hach, et al., 2016; D'Argembeau et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Strategic search abilities, such as the clustered generation of outputs on fluency or retrieval tasks, has been related to the ability to imagine specific and detailed future events <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Addis, Hach, et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">D'Argembeau et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, divergent thinking correlates with the amount of episodic detail comprising future but not past events (Addis, Pan, et al., 2016; Thakral et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Moreover, divergent thinking correlates with the amount of episodic detail comprising future but not past events <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Addis, Pan, et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Thakral et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Relational reasoning -the ability to connect disparate ideas, often via analogy (Alexander, Jablansky, et al., 2016; Holyoak, 2012) -may be particularly important for novel event generation (Addis, 2020b).
text.formatted: Relational reasoning -the ability to connect disparate ideas, often via analogy <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Alexander, Jablansky, et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Holyoak, 2012)</ref> -may be particularly important for novel event generation <ref type="bibr">(Addis, 2020b)</ref>.

text.text: Not only is performance on analogical tasks predicted by divergent thinking (Jones & Estes, 2015), analogical mapping (Gentner, 1983) is a common strategy for divergent thinking (Chrysikou & Thompson-Schill, 2011; Gubenko & Houssemand, 2022).
text.formatted: Not only is performance on analogical tasks predicted by divergent thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Jones & Estes, 2015)</ref>, analogical mapping <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Gentner, 1983</ref>) is a common strategy for divergent thinking <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Chrysikou & Thompson-Schill, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Gubenko & Houssemand, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Moreover, both relational reasoning and divergent thinking engage the rostrolateral prefrontal cortex (Christoff et al., 2001; Roberts et al., 2017) -a region that is also recruited during future simulation (Roberts et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Moreover, both relational reasoning and divergent thinking engage the rostrolateral prefrontal cortex <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Christoff et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Roberts et al., 2017)</ref> -a region that is also recruited during future simulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Roberts et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: As yet, no studies have directly tested whether analogical reasoning ability is associated with the successful simulation of future events.

In the current study, we systematically varied schema availability in a future simulation task by manipulating the congruency of location-object-object cues such that congruent locations were more effective spatial schemas than incongruent locations for integrating object cues into a coherent event.
We hypothesized that simulation would be more successful (i.e., more detailed and plausible) and more schematic on congruent versus incongruent trials.

To test this hypothesis, we applied to narrative data RSA methods traditionally used in neuroimaging (Kriegeskorte, 2008) to determine semantic similarity between future event narratives and schematic location descriptions.
text.formatted: To test this hypothesis, we applied to narrative data RSA methods traditionally used in neuroimaging <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">(Kriegeskorte, 2008)</ref> to determine semantic similarity between future event narratives and schematic location descriptions.

text.text: Because schemas reflect culturally shared knowledge (Bartlett, 1932), we had another set of participants describe what is typical in each location.
text.formatted: Because schemas reflect culturally shared knowledge <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Bartlett, 1932)</ref>, we had another set of participants describe what is typical in each location.

text.text: We applied RSA by computing cosine similarities between document embeddings for these "schema templates" and the future event narratives from the main sample using the universal sentence encoder (USE; Cer et al., 2018).
text.formatted: We applied RSA by computing cosine similarities between document embeddings for these "schema templates" and the future event narratives from the main sample using the universal sentence encoder (USE; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cer et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: We also explored whether schema use differed across the course of imagination trials.

Finally, we hypothesized that better performance on measures of analogical reasoning, divergent thinking and strategic retrieval would be associated with more successful simulation and greater schema use, especially on incongruent trials where executive demands are greater.
An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power software (Faul et al., 2009).
text.formatted: An a priori power analysis was conducted using G*Power software <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Faul et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: The analysis used a published effect size for the correlation between episodic detail and the flexibility score of the AUT (Addis, Pan, et al., 2016), and determined that a minimum of 39 participants was required to achieve a power of at least .80, with an alpha level of .05.
text.formatted: The analysis used a published effect size for the correlation between episodic detail and the flexibility score of the AUT <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Addis, Pan, et al., 2016)</ref>, and determined that a minimum of 39 participants was required to achieve a power of at least .80, with an alpha level of .05.

text.text: This result of this power analysis was reported in the pre-registration but due to a miscommunication, it misstated that the sample size would be 70.
We had aimed for a larger sample size than N = 39 given the novelty of the text analyses, but the target was N=50.
We recruited 53 young adults through the Rotman Research Institute Participant pool and community advertising.
All were fluent in English with no history or current diagnosis of psychiatric or neurological conditions.
Data from three participants were excluded due to distortions in audio recordings (n = 1) or task non-compliance (n = 2).

The final sample comprised 50 participants (sex: 35 females, 15 males; gender: 31 women, 16 men, 3 gender-diverse), aged 18-35 years (M = 23.86, SD = 4.11) with an average of 15.66 years of education (SD = 3.43).
All participants gave written informed consent prior to testing and, upon completion, received $30 CAD.
Properties of the stimuli are presented in Table 1.
text.formatted: Properties of the stimuli are presented in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>.

text.text: Stimuli were 36 nouns (12 locations and 24 objects) selected from the Glasgow Norms (Scott et al., 2019) that were high in familiarity and concreteness, and neutral to mildly positive in emotional valence.
text.formatted: Stimuli were 36 nouns (12 locations and 24 objects) selected from the Glasgow Norms <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Scott et al., 2019)</ref> that were high in familiarity and concreteness, and neutral to mildly positive in emotional valence.

text.text: These words were organized into 12 detail sets (location-object-object triplets) such that in the congruent condition, the locations would provide a schematic scaffold to integrate the objects into a coherent event whereas in the incongruent condition they would not.
Detail sets were used as cues to elicit the simulation of future events (for the list of stimuli, see Supplemental Materials, Section S1).
We matched the semantic relatedness among the words in the detail sets (pairwise cosine similarity between Word2Vec embedding's; Church, 2017) between conditions.
text.formatted: We matched the semantic relatedness among the words in the detail sets (pairwise cosine similarity between Word2Vec embedding's; <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Church, 2017)</ref> between conditions.

text.text: An independent online sample of participants (see Supplemental Materials, Section S1) reported greater ease imagining an event that integrated congruent versus incongruent detail sets (t(9.99) = 14.06, p < .001).
text.formatted: An independent online sample of participants (see Supplemental Materials, Section S1) reported greater ease imagining an event that integrated congruent versus incongruent detail sets (t(9.99) = 14.06, p < .001).

text.text: The words in the congruent and incongruent conditions did not differ in mean familiarity (t(31.48) = 1.29, p = 0.20), concreteness (t(28.03) = -1.31, p = 0.19), valence (t(33.94)= -0.62, p = .53), nor semantic similarity (t(5.05) = -1.36, p = .20).
All ratings are low to high, except for valence scale where1 = very negative;5 = neutral;9 = very positive; and ease of integration (1 = extremely difficult;7 = extremely easy).

text.text: During each trial, participants were presented with a detail set and the position of the location word (i.e., top, middle, bottom) was randomized across trials.
Participants imagined a specific future event that could plausibly take place in the next 5 years, that they would be personally involved in, and that integrated all three details together.
They were instructed to "think aloud", verbalizing everything that came to mind for 3 minutes (Wank et al., 2021).
text.formatted: They were instructed to "think aloud", verbalizing everything that came to mind for 3 minutes <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Wank et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: If they remained silent at any point during the trial, they were reminded by the experimenter to share aloud everything they were thinking, and provide as much detail about their imagined event as possible.

Participants then estimated the temporal distance of the event from the present and rated (on 5point scales where1 = low and5 = high) the amount of detail imagined, the similarity of the imagined event to their previous experiences, the event's plausibility, and the difficulty of the task.
Before starting the task, participants completed one congruent and one incongruent practice trial and explained their rating choices to confirm their comprehension of the rating scales.

The instructions, presentation of cues and rating scales, and audio-recording of each event description were programmed in PsychoPy v2022.2.5 (Peirce, 2007) and displayed on a PC desktop in white colored, 36-point font on a grey background.
text.formatted: The instructions, presentation of cues and rating scales, and audio-recording of each event description were programmed in PsychoPy v2022.2.5 <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Peirce, 2007)</ref> and displayed on a PC desktop in white colored, 36-point font on a grey background.

text.text: Each trial was audio-recorded using a desktop microphone for later transcription and analysis.

Simulation trials were excluded from analysis if the event description was not compliant with task instructions (e.g., a meaningless response was provided, not all details were integrated within the event, etc.), if the temporal distance was beyond 5 years into the future, or if the imagined event was identical to a past experience ("5" on the similarity rating scale), indicative of a memory.
We excluded two participants for whom over 50% of their trials were non-compliant.
Of the remaining analytic sample, 4% of trials were excluded from the analysis, reflecting an average of 0.12 (SD = 0.32) congruent trials and 0.36 (SD = 0.56) incongruent trials per participant.
Test of Relational Reasoning (TORR).

The TORR (Alexander, Dumas, et al., 2016) assesses four different types of fluid relational reasoning: Analogy (similarity relation), Anomaly (perceived discrepancies), Antinomy (incompatibilities), and Antithesis (dichotomies).
text.formatted: The TORR <ref type="bibr">(Alexander, Dumas, et al., 2016)</ref> assesses four different types of fluid relational reasoning: Analogy (similarity relation), Anomaly (perceived discrepancies), Antinomy (incompatibilities), and Antithesis (dichotomies).

text.text: Each of these four scales comprises 2 example and 8 visuospatial test items scored as correct (score of 1) or incorrect (score of 0).
Thus the maximum score per scale is 8, for a total score out of 32.
Qualtrics was used to present the instructions and multiple-choice question items and to collect participant responses.
Participants completed all scales, but only the Analogy subscale was used for the current analyses.
The AUT (Guilford, 1967) is a divergent thinking task that requires participants to generate alternate uses for common objects (e.g., toothpick as an alternate use for a paperclip).
text.formatted: The AUT <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Guilford, 1967)</ref> is a divergent thinking task that requires participants to generate alternate uses for common objects (e.g., toothpick as an alternate use for a paperclip).

text.text: On each of six three-minute trials, participants generated alternate uses for the target object (automobile tire, brick, button, key, paperclip and pencil).

Following each trial, participants indicated whether each of their responses was "old" (i.e., they had used or heard of it before) or "new" (i.e., they thought of it for the first time during the task; Madore et al., 2019; these data are not reported here).
text.formatted: Following each trial, participants indicated whether each of their responses was "old" (i.e., they had used or heard of it before) or "new" (i.e., they thought of it for the first time during the task; <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Madore et al., 2019</ref>; these data are not reported here).

text.text: Cues were presented and responses collected using Qualtrics.
Incomplete responses were excluded from analysis.
The scoring process followed Madore et al. (2019) and involved two steps.
text.formatted: The scoring process followed <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Madore et al. (2019)</ref> and involved two steps.

text.text: First, the appropriateness of each use response was determined according to whether it was feasible and useful in everyday life.
Inappropriate uses were excluded, as we were interested in the ability to generate plausible responses (in line with the instructions on the future simulation task).

Next, cognitive flexibility was scored for each trial by grouping the appropriate uses into distinct categories depending on whether uses involved the same physical actions, relied on the same attributes of the objects, resulted in the same type of end product or disassembly of the object.
The number of categories on each of the 6 trials were summed to provide a total cognitive flexibility score.
Inter-rater reliability was established by having two raters (S.V. and J.P.) score 24 trials randomly selected from a previous dataset (Roberts et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Inter-rater reliability was established by having two raters (S.V. and J.P.) score 24 trials randomly selected from a previous dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Roberts et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Intraclass correlation indicated high interrater reliability for the number of appropriate uses (Cronbach's α = 0.92) and number of categories per trial (Cronbach's α = 0.94).
The two raters then each scored half of the experimental trials.

For both fluency tasks, the relevant stimulus was shown onscreen and participants had one minute to list words beginning with a given letter (F, A, S) or belonging to a given category (animals, supermarket items).
Responses were audio-recorded using a desktop microphone.
Cue presentation and audio recordings were programmed in PsychoPy v2022.2.5; cues were displayed on a PC desktop.

Fluency scores were computed as the total number of words produced after excluding proper nouns, repeated words with different endings (e.g., "fall" and "falling"), and words cut off mid-response (i.e., when the trial ended).

As a measure of strategic retrieval, we computed a clustering metric whereby participants who provided responses organized as clusters of semantically or phonemically similar words were assigned a higher cluster score (for details see Troyer, 2000; Troyer et al., 1997)
text.formatted: As a measure of strategic retrieval, we computed a clustering metric whereby participants who provided responses organized as clusters of semantically or phonemically similar words were assigned a higher cluster score (for details see <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Troyer, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Troyer et al., 1997)</ref>

text.text: Testing was conducted in person.
The 2-hour session began with a brief set of demographic questions (age, biological sex, gender, years of education) and medical history related to exclusions (e.g., neurological conditions).
The future simulation task and the executive measures (TORR, AUT and verbal fluency) were separated by a brief break, and their order was counterbalanced across participants.
Audio recordings were transcribed using Google's Speech-to-Text package (implemented in Python3.11.5) using the model trained on audio from videos.
Each word in a transcript was assigned a start and end time stamp, yielding a time series of narrative production.
A research assistant reviewed transcripts while listening to the audio to correct any transcription errors and mark any interviewer comments for removal.
The amounts of episodic and non-episodic content in event narratives were quantified using the Autobiographical Interview (AI) scoring protocol (Levine et al., 2002).
text.formatted: The amounts of episodic and non-episodic content in event narratives were quantified using the Autobiographical Interview (AI) scoring protocol <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Levine et al., 2002)</ref>.

text.text: By this protocol, internal details refer to episodic content about the main episode being described in the narrative, such as event details (entities, actions, etc.), locations, perceptual details, thoughts and emotions.
External details refer to non-episodic content in the narrative, including facts, meta-cognitive statements and repetitions.

We used an automated AI scoring tool (van Genugten & Schacter, 2024) that employs distilBERT (Sanh et al., 2020) to classify each sentence in a narrative according to the percentage of internal content, which is then multiplied by the number of words in the sentence.
text.formatted: We used an automated AI scoring tool <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(van Genugten & Schacter, 2024</ref>) that employs distilBERT <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Sanh et al., 2020)</ref> to classify each sentence in a narrative according to the percentage of internal content, which is then multiplied by the number of words in the sentence.

text.text: These estimates are then aggregated across all sentences to obtain counts of the number of internal and external detail words for each narrative.
The estimates provided by this tool exhibits strong correlations with human scores (van Genugten & Schacter, 2024).
text.formatted: The estimates provided by this tool exhibits strong correlations with human scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(van Genugten & Schacter, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The degree to which a location schema was instantiated during future event simulation was quantified using narrative RSA.

Although similar approaches have recently been used for word lists (Rajaram et al., 2026) or word pairs (Walsh & Rissman, 2023) to our knowledge an RSA approach has not been applied to narratives to quantify the usage of specific knowledge structures such as schema.
text.formatted: Although similar approaches have recently been used for word lists <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Rajaram et al., 2026)</ref> or word pairs <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Walsh & Rissman, 2023)</ref> to our knowledge an RSA approach has not been applied to narratives to quantify the usage of specific knowledge structures such as schema.

text.text: To this end, we first collected descriptions of the 12 location schemas from a separate sample of participants (N = 20, aged 18-35 years, M = 27.85, SD = 4.15) recruited from Prolific.
To ensure they were members of the same collective group as the participants in the main sample, the Prolific sample only included individuals who were residents of Canada.
As in the main sample, these participants provided spoken narrative responses, albeit during a Zoom call rather than in-person.

To elicit schema descriptions, each location was presented on a PowerPoint slideshow and participants were instructed to describe each location as if they were preparing someone who had never been there: "What does it look like?
What do you typically do there?
How would you prepare to visit this location?
What would be the 'average' experience?"
Each trial lasted 90 seconds and audio was recorded using Zoom.
Audio recordings were later transcribed using Google's Speech-to-Text package using the same procedure as described above.

We used these schema description texts (N = 240; number of words: M = 198.53, SD = 55.94) and the event narrative texts from the main sample (N = 600; number of words: M = 477.89; SD = 108.60) to perform a narrative RSA quantifying the semantic similarity between event and schema descriptions.
Document embeddings were computed using the Universal Sentence Encoder (USE, version 5 Large; Cer et al., 2018) in Python (version 3.11.5), converting each text to a 512-dimensional vector.
text.formatted: Document embeddings were computed using the Universal Sentence Encoder (USE, version 5 Large; <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cer et al., 2018)</ref> in Python (version 3.11.5), converting each text to a 512-dimensional vector.

text.text: Pairwise cosine similarity was computed between all event-schema pairs and averaged for each location and condition, resulting in cross-representational similarity matrices in which each cell reflected the average semantic similarity between event and schema descriptions for a pair of locations in a condition.

This approach captures the global structure of relationships between event-specific and schema-based representations, allowing for the examination of how strongly descriptions of imagined future events align with their corresponding schemas, as well as the extent to which representations generalize across conditions.

For statistical analyses of the degree of schema use by participants in the main sample, we computed for a given event narrative its average similarity to all 20 schema descriptions for the target location minus its average similarity to all 220 non-target schema descriptions.

Subtracting the average similarity to all other schema descriptions results in more conservative estimates of schema use, but importantly this procedure controls for non-specific location knowledge as well as linguistic tendencies related to constructing narratives.
As an exploratory analysis (i.e., not pre-registered), we also quantified the usage of specific types of location schema knowledge.

From each schema description, text related to three kinds of schematic content were identified: perceptual information (i.e., visual, auditory, or olfactory experience; e.g., "I often imagine cottages as a small house, a little chimney with a small garden surrounding it.

They are usually surrounded by a forest and a lake"), preparation-related information (i.e., describing what to do before visiting the location; e.g., "We have to pack our clothes and go grocery shopping before heading to the cottage"), and action-related information (i.e., describing an event or action that can take place at this location; e.g., "We often go swimming in the lake, fish at the dock and barbeque burgers on the grill").

For each schema description, one rater (D.G.) followed the above definitions to categorize text in each schema description that belonged to either category and concatenated these extracted details for each schema description to create new descriptions representing perceptual (N = 225, number of words: M = 97.68; SD = 56.31), preparation (N = 60, number of words: M = 41.52; SD = 26.84), or action (N=210, number of words: M = 76.91; SD = 26.84) "sub-schemas".
Text unrelated to any of the three categories were labelled as miscellaneous/other (N = 24, number of words: M = 37.91; SD = 23.00) and omitted from the sub-schema analyses.
The schema use measure for each event narrative was then re-computed separately for each of these three sub-schemas.
In the preregistered analysis plan, we indicated that we would likely run an exploratory analysis to examine whether schema use is higher earlier in the future event narratives.
To this end, we conducted an exploratory sliding window analysis that quantified the time-course of schema and sub-schema use during event simulation trials.
Using the time-stamps for word onset in the event narratives, we extracted text within 60s windows with a window step size or "stride" of 30s, enabling us to compute RSA for 5 windows in total.
R (Version 4.2.2; R Core Team, 2022) was used to compute descriptive statistics, regressions and Pearson's correlations between predictor and outcome variables.
Outliers were identified using the rstatix package (Kassambara, 2023); analyses were recomputed excluding any outliers identified to confirm they were not influencing results.
Where appropriate, mixed models with a random intercept per participant were used that account for the nested structure of the data.

For analyses on ordinal outcome variables (detail and plausibility ratings), the ordinal package in R (Christensen, 2023) was used to compute cumulative link mixed models (CLMMs) with a fixed effect of condition and a random intercept per participant.
text.formatted: For analyses on ordinal outcome variables (detail and plausibility ratings), the ordinal package in R <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Christensen, 2023)</ref> was used to compute cumulative link mixed models (CLMMs) with a fixed effect of condition and a random intercept per participant.

text.text: We opted to use CLMMs as these are the statistically appropriate models for ordinal data (Liddell & Kruschke, 2018), even though our preregistration stated we would use paired samples t-tests and repeated-measures ANOVA to examine these ratings data; note that both types of analyses yielded the same pattern of results.

text.text: For continuous outcome variables (internal word counts and the schema use metrics), we used the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2015) to run linear mixed models (LMMs) with fixed effects of condition and/or schema use metrics and a random intercept per participant.

text.text: Using the afex package (Singmann et al., 2025) omnibus F tests with Satterthwaite-approximated degrees of freedom assessed the significance of fixed effects and their interactions.

text.text: Do Congruent Spatial Schemas Enhance Event Simulation?
text.formatted: <head>Do Congruent Spatial Schemas Enhance Event Simulation?
</head>

text.text: Using an LMM, we confirmed that future events in the congruent and incongruent conditions did not differ in their average temporal distance from the present (b = 37.77, t = 0.87, p = .387, β = .03, 95% CI [-0.04, 0.11]).
As manipulation checks, we computed two CLMMs on participant ratings of task difficulty and event novelty (where novelty was computed as the inverse of ratings of similarity to previous experiences).

As expected, participants gave higher difficulty ratings on incongruent trails compared to congruent trials (b = 0.47, z = 3.08, p = .002, OR = 1.61, 95% CI [1.18, 2.17]; see Supplemental Materials, Figure S1A).
text.formatted: As expected, participants gave higher difficulty ratings on incongruent trails compared to congruent trials (b = 0.47, z = 3.08, p = .002, OR = 1.61, 95% CI [1.18, 2.17]; see Supplemental Materials, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1A</ref>).

text.text: However, for novelty ratings, the difference between conditions did not reach significance, (b = 0.24, z = 1.47, p = .141, OR = 1.27, 95% CI [0.92, 1.73]; see Supplemental Materials, Figure S1B) possibly due to varying levels of personal experience with each location, regardless of the congruency manipulation.
text.formatted: However, for novelty ratings, the difference between conditions did not reach significance, (b = 0.24, z = 1.47, p = .141, OR = 1.27, 95% CI [0.92, 1.73]; see Supplemental Materials, Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1B</ref>) possibly due to varying levels of personal experience with each location, regardless of the congruency manipulation.

text.text: Simulation success was operationalized as higher detail and plausibility ratings as well as higher internal word counts reflecting more episodic content as determined by automated autobiographical interview scores (van Genugten & Schacter, 2024).
text.formatted: Simulation success was operationalized as higher detail and plausibility ratings as well as higher internal word counts reflecting more episodic content as determined by automated autobiographical interview scores <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">(van Genugten & Schacter, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: CLMM analyses found higher plausibility ratings during the congruent trials (M = 3.39) compared to incongruent trials (M = 3.08; b = -0.51, z = -3.28, p < .001, OR = 0.60, 95% CI [0.44, 0.82]; see Figure 1A).
text.formatted: CLMM analyses found higher plausibility ratings during the congruent trials (M = 3.39) compared to incongruent trials (M = 3.08; b = -0.51, z = -3.28, p < .001, OR = 0.60, 95% CI [0.44, 0.82]; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: However, the detail ratings did not differ significantly across conditions (congruent: M = 3.72; incongruent: M = 3.70; b = -0.07, z = -0.41, p = .683, OR = 0.94, 95% CI [0.68, 1.29]; see Figure 1B).
text.formatted: However, the detail ratings did not differ significantly across conditions (congruent: M = 3.72; incongruent: M = 3.70; b = -0.07, z = -0.41, p = .683, OR = 0.94, 95% CI [0.68, 1.29]; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>).

text.text: Finally, an LMM predicting internal detail with a fixed effect of condition and a random intercept per participant showed that congruent future events had significantly more internal words (M = 394.00) compared to incongruent events (M = 371.00), (b = -22.26, t = -4.09, p < .001, β = -.10, 95% CI [-.15, -.05]; see Figure 1C).

text.text: Figure 2 displays RSA similarity matrices for each condition and both the full and sub-schema templates.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref> displays RSA similarity matrices for each condition and both the full and sub-schema templates.

text.text: For the full schema templates (i.e., templates not broken down by sub-schema; top row) cosine similarity was highest between event narratives and schema templates for the same location versus different locations.
This result was confirmed using an exploratory linear regression predicting mean cosine similarity as a function of condition and whether the template and narrative locations matched.
There was a significant main effect of location match (i.e., diagonal matrix elements versus off-diagonals; b = 0.20, t = 10.82, p < .001, β = 2.91, 95% CI [2.38, 3.44]).
text.formatted: There was a significant main effect of location match (i.e., diagonal matrix elements versus off-diagonals; b = 0.20, t = 10.82, p < .001, β = 2.91, 95% CI [2.38, 3.44]).

text.text: Importantly, the similarity between event narratives and schema templates for different locations (off-diagonal elements) was also consistently greater than 0 (intercept term; b = 0.19, t = 36.57, p < .001, β = -0.34, 95% CI [-0.49, -0.18]).
text.formatted: Importantly, the similarity between event narratives and schema templates for different locations (off-diagonal elements) was also consistently greater than 0 (intercept term; b = 0.19, t = 36.57, p < .001, β = -0.34, 95% CI [-0.49, -0.18]).

text.text: As shown in the second and fourth rows of Figure 2, the same pattern is evident for the perceptual sub-schemas (diagonal vs. off-diagonal: b = 0.18, t = 9.62, p < .001, β = 2.67, 95% CI [2.12, 3.22]; off-diagonal > 0: b = 0.10, t = 20.61, p < .001, β = -0.35, 95% CI [-0.51, -0.19]) and action sub-schemas (diagonal vs. off-diagonal: b = 0.12, t = 6.40, p < .001, β = 2.04, 95% CI [1.41, 2.67]; off-diagonal > 0: b = 0.06, t = 12.15, p < .001, β = -0.26, 95% CI [-0.45, -0.08]).
text.formatted: As shown in the second and fourth rows of Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>, the same pattern is evident for the perceptual sub-schemas (diagonal vs. off-diagonal: b = 0.18, t = 9.62, p < .001, β = 2.67, 95% CI [2.12, 3.22]; off-diagonal > 0: b = 0.10, t = 20.61, p < .001, β = -0.35, 95% CI [-0.51, -0.19]) and action sub-schemas (diagonal vs. off-diagonal: b = 0.12, t = 6.40, p < .001, β = 2.04, 95% CI [1.41, 2.67]; off-diagonal > 0: b = 0.06, t = 12.15, p < .001, β = -0.26, 95% CI [-0.45, -0.08]).

text.text: For the preparation sub-schema (third row of Figure 3) this pattern is less visually evident, but the comparison between diagonal versus off-diagonal elements was still statistically significant (b = 0.04, t = 4.65, p < .001, β = 1.84, 95% CI [1.06, 2.62]) and the offdiagonal elements were consistently greater than 0 (b = 0.01, t = 2.72, p = .007, β = -0.13, 95% CI [-0.36, 0.09]).

text.text: Thus, event narratives exhibited a significant degree of similarity to all schema templates (regardless of location), justifying our approach to computing schema use as described above: we computed the schema use for an event narrative as its selective similarity to schema templates for the cued location while controlling (via subtraction) for its similarity to schema templates for all other non-cued locations.
This selective similarity metric was used as the measure of schema use for all subsequent analyses.

An LMM demonstrated that overall schema use was higher for narratives in the congruent (M = 0.20) compared to incongruent condition (M = 0.18; b = -0.01, t = -2.79, p = .005, β = -0.11, 95% CI [-0.19, -0.03]); Figure 3A).
text.formatted: An LMM demonstrated that overall schema use was higher for narratives in the congruent (M = 0.20) compared to incongruent condition (M = 0.18; b = -0.01, t = -2.79, p = .005, β = -0.11, 95% CI [-0.19, -0.03]); Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3A</ref>).

text.text: Importantly, this result indicated that, as predicted, event narratives were more schematic when the location was congruent with two object cues.
In an exploratory set of analyses, we also computed an LMM predicting schema use with condition (congruent, incongruent) and sub-schema type (perceptual, action, preparation) as factors.
This analysis revealed that schema use varied significantly by sub-schema type (F(2, 1678.9) = 95.89, p < .001, η² p = 0.10).
text.formatted: This analysis revealed that schema use varied significantly by sub-schema type (F(2, 1678.9) = 95.89, p < .001, η² p = 0.10).

text.text: Bonferroni-corrected pairwise contrasts revealed that, overall, participants had significantly higher perceptual (M = 0.16) compared to preparation schema use (M = 0.11; b = 0.05, t =12.91, p < .001), and significantly higher action (M = 0.15) compared to preparation schema use (b = 0.04, t = 10.79, p < .001).
text.formatted: Bonferroni-corrected pairwise contrasts revealed that, overall, participants had significantly higher perceptual (M = 0.16) compared to preparation schema use (M = 0.11; b = 0.05, t =12.91, p < .001), and significantly higher action (M = 0.15) compared to preparation schema use (b = 0.04, t = 10.79, p < .001).

text.text: There was no significant difference between perceptual and action schema use (b = 0.01, t = 2.12, p = .102).
There was also no significant main effect of condition (F(1, 1682.29) = 3.53, p = .060).
However, there was a significant condition-by-schematype interaction (F(2, 1678.93) = 73.58, p < .001, η² p = 0.08, 95% CI [0.06, 0.11]).
text.formatted: However, there was a significant condition-by-schematype interaction (F(2, 1678.93) = 73.58, p < .001, η² p = 0.08, 95% CI [0.06, 0.11]).

text.text: Bonferronicorrected pairwise contrasts found that perceptual schema use did not differ between conditions (b = -0.01, t = -1.20, p = .232; see Figure 3B).

text.text: However, preparation schema use was higher in the congruent (M = 0.14) than the incongruent condition (M = 0.08; b = 0.06, t = 10.57, p < .001), whereas action schema use was higher in the incongruent (M = 0.14) than the congruent condition (M = 0.17; b = -0.03, t = -6.12, p < .001; Figure 3C-D, respectively).

text.text: To determine whether schema use was higher at the start of simulation trials, we implemented a sliding window time-course analysis.
From each event narrative, we extracted text within 60-s windows (with a window step size or "stride" of 30s), resulting in 5 time windows across the 180s trials.
We re-computed the RSA analyses, comparing each time window to the schema templates.

The resulting cosine similarity data (controlling for similarity to all non-cued locations as described above) for the full schema templates and all three sub-schemas were then entered into separate LMMs which, along with the effect of condition, included predictors for time window and the condition by time-window interaction (see Table 2 for results).
text.formatted: The resulting cosine similarity data (controlling for similarity to all non-cued locations as described above) for the full schema templates and all three sub-schemas were then entered into separate LMMs which, along with the effect of condition, included predictors for time window and the condition by time-window interaction (see Table <ref type="table">2</ref> for results).

text.text: In addition to the main effects of condition on schema use described in the previous section, these analyses indicated a main effect of time window for the use of the full schema and all three sub-schemas (all F values > 44.70, p values < .001; see Figure 4).
text.formatted: In addition to the main effects of condition on schema use described in the previous section, these analyses indicated a main effect of time window for the use of the full schema and all three sub-schemas (all F values > 44.70, p values < .001; see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>).

text.text: We computed Bonferroni-corrected planned comparisons of adjacent time windows (i.e., windows starting at 0 vs. 30s, 30s vs. 60s etc.)

These results indicated that for all schema types, there was a significant reduction in usage between the first (0-60s) and second (30-90s) time windows (p values < .001), which plateaued by the end of the trial with no differences between the fourth (90-150s) and fifth (120-180s) time windows (p values > .831; see Figure 4; for full statistics, see Supplemental Materials Table S10).

text.text: However there were differences between schema types for the intervening time windows.

For full and perceptual schema, significant reductions were also evident between the second to third (full: p = .002; perceptual, p = .002) and third to fourth (full: p = .008; perceptual, p = .027) time windows.

For action and preparation schema, the reductions from the second to third time windows did not reach significance except for action schema between the third to fourth time window (p = .043; all other p values, .056 -.108).

Whether the use of the full schema and sub-schemas influenced simulation success was tested 12 using CLMMs for detail and plausibility ratings and an LMM for internal word count.

Contrary to 13 our hypotheses, none of the schema use metrics predicted detail ratings (all p values > .559) or 14 internal word counts (p values > .161; for full statistics, see Table S4-6 in Supplemental Materials).
text.formatted: Contrary to 13 our hypotheses, none of the schema use metrics predicted detail ratings (all p values > .559) or 14 internal word counts (p values > .161; for full statistics, see Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>-6 in Supplemental Materials).

text.text: However, action schema use was positively associated with plausibility (b = 11.24, z = 2.76, p = 16 .006, OR = 7.64×10⁴, 95% CI [26.24, 2.23×10⁸).
This effect was moderated by condition (b = -17 4.93, z = -2.11, p = .035, OR = 0.01, 95% CI [0.0001, 0.7101]).

Follow-up simple slope analyses indicated that greater action schema use was associated with higher plausibility ratings in the congruent (b = 6.32, z = 3.26, p = .001, OR = 553.27, 95% CI [5.36, 5.72×10⁴]) but not the incongruent condition (b = 1.39, z = 1.01, p = .313, OR = 138.14, 95% CI [0.51, 3.74×10⁴]).

Before examining the contribution of executive functions to schema use and simulation success, we determined whether the measures from the TORR, AUT and fluency tasks could be collapsed into a single latent variable (as per our pre-registration plan).

Although there was a positive correlation between semantic and phonemic clustering scores (r = .35, p = .013), this did not survive a Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons (α = .008), and no other correlations between executive measures were significant (p values > .118; see Table S2 in Supplemental Materials).

text.text: Thus, we computed separate analyses using each executive measure as a predictor.

LMM analyses revealed no significant effects of any of the executive measures on the use of the full schema or sub-schemas use (all p values > .483; see Table S3 in Supplemental Materials), nor were there any significant interaction effects between executive measures and condition (all p values > .439).

text.text: The effect of each executive measure on simulation success was estimated using CLMMs for detail and plausibility ratings and an LMM for internal word count (for full statistical results, see Tables S7-9 Supplemental Materials).

text.text: We found that greater analogical reasoning abilities were associated with higher detail ratings (b = 0.51, z = 2.75, p = .006, OR = 1.66, 95% CI [1.16, 2.38]).
text.formatted: We found that greater analogical reasoning abilities were associated with higher detail ratings (b = 0.51, z = 2.75, p = .006, OR = 1.66, 95% <ref type="bibr">CI [1.16,</ref> <ref type="bibr">2.38]</ref>).

text.text: Interestingly, this effect was moderated by condition (b = -0.22, z = -2.41, p = .016, OR = 0.80, 95% CI [0.67, 0.96]).

Follow-up simple slope analyses indicated that greater analogical reasoning abilities were associated with higher detail ratings in the congruent condition (b = 0.29, z = 2.17 p = .030, OR = 1.34, 95% CI [1.03, 1.73]) but not in the incongruent condition (b = 0.07, z = 0.54, p = .592, OR = 1.07, 95% CI [0.83, 1.40]).

However, no other executive measure was significantly associated with detail ratings (p values > .488), and none of the executive measures had effects on plausibility ratings (p values > .116) or internal word count (p values >.572).
